questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of discontinuous variation in humans?

options.text: Height
Body mass
ABO blood group
Skin colour

questions.explanation: A person is A, B, AB or O with nothing in between, so blood group falls into clear-cut categories controlled by one gene and unaffected by the environment. Height, mass and skin colour are polygenic and environmentally influenced, giving a smooth range of values.

distractorRationale.a: Height varies smoothly and is affected by diet as well as by many genes
distractorRationale.b: Body mass is strongly influenced by diet and activity
distractorRationale.d: Skin colour is polygenic and grades continuously between extremes

questions.stem: The sex of a human child is determined by

options.text: the mother, because she carries the developing baby
the father, because only he produces both X-bearing and Y-bearing gametes
the diet of the mother during pregnancy
the number of chromosomes in the egg cell

questions.explanation: A mother is XX and every egg she produces carries an X. A father is XY and produces X and Y sperm in equal numbers, so whether the child is XX or XY depends entirely on which of his sperm reaches the egg first.

distractorRationale.a: Carrying the pregnancy has no bearing on which sperm fertilised the egg
distractorRationale.c: Diet cannot alter the sex chromosome already present in the zygote
distractorRationale.d: All normal eggs carry 23 chromosomes, one of which is always an X

questions.stem: Two parents both have the sickle cell trait (genotype AS). What is the probability that any one of their children will have sickle cell anaemia?

options.text: 1 in 4
1 in 2
3 in 4

questions.explanation: The cross AS × AS gives offspring in the ratio 1 AA : 2 AS : 1 SS, so one quarter are expected to be SS and therefore to have sickle cell anaemia. Half will carry the trait like their parents and a quarter will be entirely normal.

distractorRationale.a: Both parents carry the S allele, so an SS child is possible
distractorRationale.c: 1 in 2 would be the proportion with the trait, AS, not with the disease
distractorRationale.d: 3 in 4 is the proportion who will not have the disease

questions.stem: A couple have had three daughters. What is the probability that their fourth child will be a son?

options.text: Certain, because they are due a son
1 in 2, because each fertilisation is an independent event
1 in 4, because they already have three girls
3 in 4, because the chance increases with each girl

questions.explanation: Whether an X-bearing or a Y-bearing sperm fertilises the egg is decided afresh at each conception, and the two kinds are produced in equal numbers. Previous pregnancies leave no trace on the process, so the probability remains one half every time.

distractorRationale.a: Biology keeps no record of past outcomes, so nothing is ever due
distractorRationale.c: This confuses the chance of four girls in a row with the chance for one particular child
distractorRationale.d: The probability does not accumulate across pregnancies

questions.stem: Colour blindness is much commoner in men than in women because the allele is

options.text: dominant and carried on the Y chromosome
recessive and carried on the X chromosome, and a man has only one X
found only in male body cells
caused by a shortage of vitamin A in men

questions.explanation: A woman has two X chromosomes, so a normal allele on one X masks a faulty allele on the other and she is only a carrier. A man has a single X and a Y that lacks the corresponding gene, so one faulty allele is enough to make him colour blind.

distractorRationale.a: The allele is recessive and lies on the X, not the Y
distractorRationale.c: Women carry the allele too, but usually without expressing it
distractorRationale.d: Colour blindness is inherited, unlike night blindness which is caused by vitamin A deficiency

questions.stem: A person of blood group AB has both A and B antigens on the surface of the red cells. This is because the alleles for A and B are

options.text: codominant, so both are fully expressed
both recessive
incompletely dominant, giving an intermediate antigen
carried on the sex chromosomes

questions.explanation: Codominance means neither allele masks the other and both products appear, so a person with one allele for A and one for B makes both antigens. This differs from incomplete dominance, where the heterozygote shows a genuinely intermediate phenotype.

distractorRationale.b: Both are dominant to the O allele, so neither is recessive
distractorRationale.c: There is no blended intermediate antigen; both antigens are present separately
distractorRationale.d: The ABO gene lies on an autosome, not on a sex chromosome

questions.stem: Why has the sickle cell allele remained common in parts of West Africa despite the severity of sickle cell anaemia?

options.text: Because SS individuals are especially healthy
Because AS carriers have some resistance to malaria and so survive to reproduce
Because the allele is dominant
Because the allele arose only recently

questions.explanation: Heterozygotes are usually healthy and are less severely affected by malaria than AA individuals, so in malarial regions they have a survival advantage and pass the S allele on. Natural selection therefore keeps the allele at a substantial frequency even though SS individuals suffer greatly.

distractorRationale.a: SS individuals suffer painful crises, anaemia and a reduced life expectancy
distractorRationale.c: The allele behaves as recessive for the disease; only SS individuals are affected
distractorRationale.d: The allele is ancient, and recency would not explain a high frequency

questions.stem: Continuous variation such as height is influenced by both many genes and the environment.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: True. Height is polygenic, so many genes each make a small contribution and the combined effect produces a smooth range rather than distinct categories. Nutrition, illness in childhood and other environmental factors then modify the outcome, which is why identical twins raised differently can differ in height.

questions.stem: A poultry farmer keeps and breeds only from the hens that lay the most eggs, generation after generation. This practice is called

options.text: natural selection
selective breeding
vegetative propagation
genetic counselling

questions.explanation: The farmer, rather than the environment, decides which individuals reproduce, so the alleles for high egg production become progressively commoner in the flock. It depends entirely on the existence of inherited variation among the hens to select from.

distractorRationale.a: In natural selection the environment does the selecting, with no human choice involved
distractorRationale.c: Vegetative propagation is asexual reproduction in plants
distractorRationale.d: Genetic counselling advises people about the risk of passing on a genetic disorder

questions.stem: Using a genetic cross, show why a man and a woman who both have the genotype AS have a one in four chance of producing a child with sickle cell anaemia. Explain why genotype testing before marriage is advised in Nigeria, and state the advantage the AS genotype confers.
markingGuide: Symbols defined: A is the allele for normal haemoglobin, S the allele for sickle haemoglobin (1 mark)
Parental genotypes stated as AS and AS, both with sickle cell trait (1 mark)
Gametes shown: each parent produces A and S gametes in equal numbers (2 marks)
Punnett square or cross correctly giving AA, AS, AS and SS (3 marks)
Ratio interpreted: 1 AA normal : 2 AS trait : 1 SS sickle cell anaemia, so a one in four risk at every pregnancy (2 marks)

Reason for testing: the couple can be informed of the recurring risk before starting a family and make decisions with full knowledge, since the risk applies afresh to each pregnancy rather than only once in four children (2 marks)
Advantage of AS: heterozygotes have increased resistance to malaria, which is why the allele has persisted in malarial regions (1 mark)
questions.explanation: The cross AS × AS yields 1 AA : 2 AS : 1 SS, so the one in four risk is a probability that applies independently to each pregnancy rather than a guarantee of one affected child in four. Testing matters because both carriers are healthy and would otherwise have no way of knowing the risk, and the persistence of the allele is explained by the malaria resistance of the AS genotype.
